title: Success isn’t linear. What I wish I knew at 29.
guest: Michelle Huang, Head of Special Projects at TikTok; former private equity and growth equity investor at Blackstone, former office of the CEO at Loro Piana, Stanford GSB graduate
summary: Cherie interviews Michelle Huang at a 2024 conference about advice for her 29-year-old self, a failure she is grateful for, first jobs and travel, then the sisters debrief. Michelle's core message is patience: life is long and nonlinear, good things happen to good people at different times, and the way to change the course of your life is to embrace what is in front of you. The sisters relate it to Jean leaving Snap and ending an eight-year engagement in 2024, Jean's failed 2016 startup, and the happiness-equals-reality-minus-expectations formula.

ideas.idea: The advice for a 29-year-old is to be more patient: life is nonlinear, good things happen to good people at different stages, and you will have your own moment even if you do not know when.
ideas.detail: Right after Stanford GSB Michelle was anxious to join the next big thing and be part of everything her peers were doing; that drive was good for ambition but bad for mental health. The years around 29 are the most painful because of anticipation, and once you cross 30 life goes on and is great.

ideas.idea: Life is so long that people reinvent themselves all the time and hit their stride at different times; a friend's timeline is not the best timeline for you.
ideas.detail: Jean quotes Michelle directly and adds that just because something did not happen for you at the same time as your friends does not mean it will not happen.

ideas.idea: The failure she is most grateful for was at 26 when she broke up with her longtime boyfriend and was rejected from Harvard Business School in the same fall, shattering her planned life.
ideas.detail: Her plan was HBS while he attended Harvard Medical School, then marriage and a white-picket-fence house in Boston; she ended up at Stanford GSB instead. The lesson was resilience and how to bounce back and change course.

ideas.idea: Replace 'where there's a will there's a way' with 'embrace what's in front of you and keep going on the path you're on' as the way to change the course of your life.
ideas.detail: Michelle moved from forcing outcomes to believing in what is meant to be; the hosts close the episode on her line 'How do you change the course of your life? Embrace what's in front of you.'

ideas.idea: Good things happen to good people, but only over the long run; cutting corners can pay off short term but loses over a long time horizon.
ideas.detail: Michelle's stated hot take, tied to keeping a long-term mentality about how you treat people and do things.

ideas.idea: Scandinavians are the happiest people in the world because they have low expectations, so a rare sunny day after a long winter brings real joy.
ideas.detail: Michelle spent two weeks across Stockholm and Copenhagen in summer and asked locals the secret; the hosts turn it into the formula happiness equals reality minus expectations, so lower expectations plus decent reality yields happiness.

ideas.idea: Being thrown into brand-new fields in your first jobs gives you the lasting confidence that you can pick anything up.
ideas.detail: Michelle did consulting for under a year, which felt like being paid to learn on a playground, then joined private equity in New York and Hong Kong with no finance background while her cohort had built models before; being behind on day one taught her a growth mindset. Jean adds that if you stop learning and growing it is the death knell of curiosity.

ideas.idea: The most valuable conferences have no industry agenda and simply bring interesting people from different walks of life together so connections form organically.
ideas.detail: Michelle contrasts Conference 2024 with investor-, entrepreneur- or healthcare-specific events; Cherie agrees the dinner conversations with people she would never normally meet held the most learning.

ideas.idea: For ambitious people work life and personal life are intertwined, so a personal rupture reshapes a career and vice versa.
ideas.detail: The hosts note Michelle was one of the few guests to bring her personal life into a career conversation; Jean relates it to 2024, when she left her seven-year corporate job as head of product at Snapchat and ended an eight-year relationship and engagement, leaving her asking 'who am I?' when identity was tied to both title and partner.

ideas.idea: Failing at something once does not mean you are not destined for it; get back on the horse with more experience.
ideas.detail: Jean's current startup is her second: she ran a startup full-time in 2016 with customers and a team and shut it down after a year because it was not the path she wanted after business school. Since then she has done $100 million deals, run major teams and built business units. Guest Vu similarly did Y Combinator at 18-19 and again at 22-23 and called the two a world of difference.

ideas.idea: Let go of dreams that were not meant for you so you can receive future opportunities instead of staring at the closed door.
ideas.detail: Cherie paraphrases a Helen Keller quote that when one door closes another opens, but you must look for the open window rather than the closed door; she and Michelle both subscribe to the idea that what will happen will happen, a belief leaders hold but rarely discuss publicly.

ideas.idea: A strong school culture like Stanford GSB or Dartmouth creates an almost compulsive familial bond between alumni that opens conversations anywhere.
ideas.detail: At the conference dinner Cherie found the GSB alumni network far larger than she expected, with shared classes and inside jokes providing instant common ground; Jean says Dartmouth alumni have the same compulsion to talk about the school together.
